messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 49
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Fashion Designer
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Future Plans: Making any plans for the future, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Memory: Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Matthias Brenner is a 49-year-old European-American fashion designer who has been married for twenty-two years and has built a career around precision, beauty, and the careful construction of things that last. He presents for treatment approximately fourteen months after the event that, by his own account, divided his life into two irreconcilable halves.

On a Sunday afternoon in early autumn, Matthias's seventeen-year-old son, Luca, was struck by a vehicle while cycling near their home in a suburb outside Chicago. Matthias was not present at the moment of impact, but he arrived at the scene within minutes, having received a call from a neighbor. What he found — Luca unconscious on the asphalt, a spreading dark stain beneath his helmet, the bicycle wheel still spinning — became the material around which his inner life has since reorganized itself entirely. Luca survived, but spent eleven days in intensive care and sustained a traumatic brain injury that has permanently altered his speech and fine motor function. Matthias stood at the roadside that afternoon, spoke to the paramedics, held his son's hand in the ambulance, and then, at some point he cannot fully account for, he was in a hospital waiting room. The gap between those two moments remains one of the most distressing features of his recall. Some images from that day are engraved with terrible clarity — the spinning wheel, the particular gray of the pavement, the paramedic's orange gloves — while other stretches are simply absent, and he cannot determine whether he said the right things, did the right things, or whether there was a moment in which he could have acted differently. He had come to believe, with a conviction that resisted all counter-evidence, that there was something he had failed to do or say, some intervention he had missed, and that this failure was the defining moral fact of his life.

In the months that followed, Matthias found that certain features of his ordinary working environment had become unbearable. He is a designer whose studio is located in the city's garment district, and his work regularly involves courier deliveries, fabric shipments arriving by van, and the constant movement of vehicles on the street below his studio windows. On several occasions, the sound of a delivery truck braking sharply outside, or the sight of a cyclist passing on the street, produced in him an immediate and violent physical response — his heart would seize, his hands would shake, and he would find himself gripping the edge of his drafting table, unable to speak to the assistants around him. He began scheduling his most important client meetings for rooms at the back of the building, away from street-facing windows, and over several months his staff came to assume this was simply a preference. It was not. He had also stopped attending the regular industry events and seasonal planning meetings that had previously anchored his professional calendar. When colleagues proposed collaborative projects or asked him to commit to collections twelve months out, he found himself unable to respond. The idea of making plans — of imagining a future in which he was present and functional — felt to him like a kind of presumption he no longer had the right to make.

At home, he described keeping himself relentlessly occupied: working late, filling evenings with administrative tasks, watching television programs he had no interest in, anything to prevent the stillness in which the memory could surface. When it did surface, the emotional force of it was such that he could not remain with it for more than a few seconds before needing to stop entirely — to leave the room, to splash water on his face, to find some task. He slept poorly, lying awake in the early hours with a heaviness he could not name as anything other than shame.

What finally brought Matthias to seek help was a conversation with his wife, who told him quietly one evening that she felt she had lost him too. He wept, which surprised him. He came to the first session saying he was not sure therapy could help someone who had simply not done enough. What he hoped for, he said, was to be able to look at his son without feeling that he was the reason Luca's life had been diminished.
